body_markdown:
It is a cold, steel-grey day at Mercedes-Benz Immendingen test track, near Stuttgart. Fortunately, it’s a dry one. Conversation is cooking with Ola Kallenius, M-B’s maximum boss, when one of his 160,000 employees arrives to tell me that the Mercedes-AMG CLE 646 *Spezialanfertigung* is ready to drive. The clocks went back the day before, the light will soon fade, and I really don’t want to be driving a car of this value and rarity on an unfamiliar track in the dark. “You should go,” says Kallenius. “This will be your last chance today to drive it. In fact, we probably won’t let any other media drive it, so this might be your last chance for the rest of your life.”


No point inviting other media to drive it because Mercedes-AMG has none left to sell. Only 30 of these cars will be made, a figure low even by comparison with the many limited-run specials we’ve seen from more exotic super- and hypercar makers of late. Aston Martin is making 150 Valens, and Gordon Murray is making 64 examples of its S1. Like those cars, the 646 sold out before it was unveiled in September, even at its lofty price—not confirmed but rumored to be around $800,000. We invite AMG to correct us.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Once you’ve figured out how *Spezialanfertigung* is pronounced (the name was reportedly chosen by the engineers and means “special production”), the next step is understanding how a car like this drives. Though at $800K, many might consider the entire exercise to be an irrelevant, billionaire’s bauble. (And never homologated for the United States, anyway.)


## Specs: 2027 Mercedes-AMG CLE 646


**Price:** $800,000 (estimated)
**Powertrain:** 4.0-liter, flat-plane-crank, twin-turbocharged V-8 with 48V mild hybrid, 9-speed automatic transmission
**Output:** 637 hp at 6000 rpm; 626 lb-ft of torque between 2500 and 4500 rpm
**Layout:** Front-engine, two-door, two-passenger, rear-drive coupe
**Weight:** 4177 lbs
**0 to 60 mph:** 3.9 seconds
**EPA-rated Fuel Economy:** N/A
**Competitors:** None, really


Mercedes-Benz AG


That perspective fails to capture a critical point for Mercedes buffs: The CLE 646 proves that AMG’s code M177 Evo twin-turbo V-8 engine fits under the hood of the CLE and, thus, the related C-Class. Remember that the 2.0-liter, four-cylinder engine—with plug-in hybrid power—in the outgoing AMG C 63 was technically impressive but unengaging despite its 671 hp. Production quietly ended earlier this year, leaving AMG without a BMW M3 competitor. The hottest CLE around showrooms is the 53, a mid-tier performance machine, using a 3.0-liter hybrid inline-six. In gastronomic terms, the 646 is an hors d’œuvre as much as a special—a physical indication (beyond the rumors) that AMG is expected to return to V-8 power in its smaller cars.


So, before we get to the drive, what does $800,000 buy from Affalterbach’s special cellar? The 646’s flat-plane-crank V-8 isn’t some race- or hypercar exotic but a development of the engine first introduced earlier this year in the S-Class. In addition to improving throttle response, a flat-plane design runs more efficiently, and Mercedes’ main reason for adopting it for regular road cars was to meet tough emissions regulations.


Flat-plane designs also typically produce more treble than the bass we usually associate with AMGs, but in all applications this engine uses variable cam profiles at lower revs to bring back the burble, further enhanced for the 646 by a custom exhaust from Akrapovic. The engine has been tuned to make 637 hp (the 646 refers to the horsepower output in PS), which is a fairly gentle 107-hp uplift over the standard engine in the S-Class. It makes 626 lb-ft of torque between 2500 and 4500 rpm, but the redline is a conservative 6800 rpm. The Mercedes-made Speedshift nine-speed torque converter transmission remains.

Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


The rest of the 646 has received a more dramatic makeover. Weight drops by 375 pounds, though it’s still no lightweight at 4177 pounds. The 4Matic four-wheel drive system has been stripped out, most of the body panels are now carbon fiber (partly because new ones were required to accommodate a 2.3-inch increase in track) and the rear and side windows are now polycarbonate, a sure sign of a proper skunkworks special. There is a vast new front grille and ducts to cool the engine and brakes, and both the front splitter and that broad rear wing are adjustable. The car rides 0.86 of an inch lower at the front, and 0.63 of an inch lower at the rear on bespoke, adjustable coilovers from KW, and the 16.5-inch carbon-ceramic front are gripped by six-piston calipers. The Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R tires on 20-inch rims are unique to this machine; they are a development of the rubber created for AMG’s One hypercar.


Inside, AMG dumped the rear seats, and there are new carbon race seats up front along with a roll cage. The dashboard and controls are familiar from the CLE 53 but the audio, comfort, and safety systems have been thinned out to suit the focus of the car, as has the sound deadening. There are no parking sensors.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


I was only able to drive the car on Immendingen’s handling circuit, but Mercedes says the CLE 646 is intended for fast road and track use. Immendingen does a pretty good impersonation of an Alpine road in places. As you settle into the cockpit (with the optional six-point harness, that can take a while), the contrast between the familiar luxury bits from the CLE and race-car details like the carbon door panels and fabric door pulls tell you you’re in something special. Noise and vibration underscore every moment behind the wheel, but it’s the good kind, welcome in raw AMG car.


Unlike some other such specials, this model’s weight still limits just how much sharper and lighter the 646 can feel. It compensates with a setup that grips and corners with race-car-like hardness and flatness. It’s not quite the real deal, but close enough to feel substantially different to a standard production car without spoiling the road manners. There isn’t a huge amount of feel from the steering but it’s weighty and consistent. You can put the nose pretty much anywhere you want it. AMG’s nine-stage traction control system is present, and that’s a good thing. You can progressively reduce its degree of assistance, and AMG’s intermediate settings allow you to generate and hold decent slip angles without risking a red face at a track day.


It’s all brilliantly engineered and very flattering to the driver, but the 646 is missing some of the fizz and fun you’d hope for from such a rare thing. That’s partly down to the engine. It sounds great—just like an AMG V-8 should—but could do with an even louder sound and higher revs, so you can enjoy that noise for longer. The nine-speed gearbox probably doesn’t help here; sure, you’re more likely to be in the perfect gear, but sometimes technically perfect is not the point. Holding gears for longer or making bigger steps on downshifts might dial up the fun.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


I hesitate to say this, but it’s also not that fast. Yes, it will hit 60 mph in 3.9 seconds and go on to a top speed of 193 mph. But speed is everywhere these days; prior to the CLE 646 I had just driven, way ahead of the international media launch, the new electric AMG GT63 SUV, now the world’s most powerful production SUV with a peak power output of 1153 hp. It has a 60-mph sprint time of 2.5 seconds, despite its 6000-pound weight.


Sure, a car like the 646 is meant to be the antidote to that sort of bonkers (but ultimately digital and uninvolving) acceleration, but once that experience is in one’s memory, the violence of it can’t be unlearnt. Despite its high price, low volumes, and the thoroughness with which it has been re-engineered, the 646 doesn’t fully capitalize on the advantages of internal combustion, which are the ability to go properly lightweight (in the absence of a battery) and fully feral with the engine.


Mercedes-Benz AG


The outlandish price likely skews expectations. If Mercedes-AMG had positioned it as a Black Series car at less than half this price, hell yes. But at more than the price of a V-12 Ferrari or Lamborghini, I’m not so sure. Rarity alone doesn’t justify the value, but the AMG completists who have ordered the 646 doubtless won’t care. On the upside, those of us who might hope to lease the future CLE 63—which one assumes this car presages—should be very glad that it exists.


## 2027 Mercedes-AMG CLE 646 *Spezialanfertigung*


**Highs:** Extreme rarity, striking looks, endless adjustability, and proper skunkworks feel.


**Lows:** Not as quick or as raw as the price and rarity demand.


**Takeaway:** We’re glad it exists, but it’s difficult to justify the CLE 646 in any rational terms.
